brief: Please turn my review of pull request #318, Skip reminders for cancelled visits, into a page. I'm the tech lead at Oakmere Clinics and the author is Ines Varga. She will open it on her laptop from a link I paste into our team chat, so each note must sit right beside the line it is about. The changed code, with line numbers: 12: def due_reminders(visits, now): 13:     out = [] 14:     for v in visits: 15:         if v.status == 'cancelled': 16:             continue 17:         gap = hours_between(now, v.start) 18:         if gap <= 24: 19:             out.append(v) 20:     return out [end of code]. My notes. Line 15: correct, but a rescheduled visit keeps the status booked for ten minutes, so a stale reminder can still go out (must fix). Line 17: a visit already in the past gives a negative gap, which passes the check on line 18 (must fix, add a test). Line 18: 24 hours is hard-coded and the clinics agreed 36 for Fridays (suggestion). Line 20: neat and easy to read (praise). Open with the verdict, changes requested, and mark which notes block the merge: two must-fix, one suggestion, one praise. Say her four new tests pass.

I run the programme office at Halvern Water, and I need the full report on moving our customer billing from the old system to the new one, for the audit committee, who will print it and also open it on laptops at the meeting on 2026-11-12. It should read like a forty-page report: a one-page summary first, a contents list, six chapters, then four appendices. Chapters: 1 Scope (214 account groups, 1.9 million customer records). 2 Method: moved region by region, with a rehearsal before each wave. 3 Cutover waves: wave 1 on 2026-03-14, wave 2 on 2026-06-20, wave 3 on 2026-09-12. 4 Data quality: 98.7% of records matched first time, 24,300 were fixed by hand. 5 Cost: £4.2m spent against a £3.9m budget. 6 Lessons and open risks: the old meter feed switches off on 2026-12-31, and 1,180 duplicate accounts remain. Appendices: A record counts for each wave, B the 31 data checks, C the interface list, D a glossary. The appendices are reference, so say plainly that the committee may skip them. The summary and chapters 5 and 6 are what they must read, because they are asked to approve the £0.3m overspend.

People keep asking where the exact values live, so I want a reference page for the design tokens of Fernlight, our household-bills app; I lead its design systems. Engineers will keep it open on a second screen while they work, and designers will get it as a link pasted into chat. Group the tokens as Colour, Spacing, Type and Corners, each with its name, its value and one line on when to use it. Colour: brand.primary Fern Green #2F7D4F; brand.accent Marigold #F2B134; surface.base Chalk #FAF8F3; surface.raised White #FFFFFF; text.main Soot #1E2420; text.muted Slate #5C655F; danger Brick #B3392B. Spacing in pixels: space.1 4, space.2 8, space.3 12, space.4 16, space.6 24, space.8 32. Type in pixels, size/line height: body 16/24, caption 13/18, title 22/28, display 34/40. Corners in pixels: radius.small 4, radius.card 12, radius.pill 999. Show each colour as a swatch next to its code and make the names easy to copy. Include the rule that text.muted must not be used on surface.raised below 14 pixels. When the link is shared it should be described as: Every colour, space and type size in Fernlight, with the value and when to use it.

As Tallybook's security engineer I have to present my review of the settings file for its billing service, which launches on 2026-11-03, at the go/no-go review on Thursday 2026-10-22. The page will be projected, so the verdict must read at a glance and each finding must be tied to the numbered line it is about. The file, by line: 1 listen = 0.0.0.0:8080. 2 admin_listen = 0.0.0.0:9000. 3 debug = true. 4 tls = off. 5 session_secret = changeme-2024. 6 session_hours = 720. 7 db_user = root. 8 db_password = tally123. 9 allowed_origins = *. 10 log_bodies = true. 11 backup_bucket = public-read. 12 rate_limit = 0. Findings. Critical: line 4, traffic is not encrypted; lines 7 and 8, root with a guessable password; line 11, backups readable by anyone. High: line 5, a default secret anyone can guess; line 2, admin port open to every network; line 10, card details end up in logs. Medium: lines 3, 9 and 12. Low: line 6, sessions last 30 days. Open with the verdict, do not ship, and the counts: three critical, three high, three medium, one low. For each finding show the line, the fix, the owner and the due date. Dana Reyes owns lines 2 to 6, Jun Takeda lines 7 to 12, all due 2026-10-28.

Partner developers keep asking us the same questions about reserving a locker, so I want a page that explains the booking API of Marlow Lockers, which runs parcel lockers in office buildings; I lead its developer relations. They will read it on a laptop at their desk after following a link from our partner chat, so it must walk through the flow in order and not just list calls. Flow. 1. Reserve: POST /v1/holds with a locker size (S, M or L) and a building code; the answer gives a hold id and a drop code, and the hold lasts 15 minutes. 2. Extend: POST /v1/holds/{id}/extend adds 15 minutes, at most twice, so 45 minutes in all. 3. Confirm: POST /v1/holds/{id}/confirm once the courier has dropped the parcel, which issues the pickup code, valid 72 hours. 4. Release: DELETE /v1/holds/{id} frees the locker. Errors: 409 locker_taken, 410 hold_expired, 429 slow_down (limit 60 requests per minute per partner key). Add a glossary appendix at the end for these terms: hold, drop code, pickup code, building code, partner key, release. Each entry is one or two plain sentences. The first time each term appears in the explanation it should lead the reader to its entry.

On 2026-10-27 I present, as their brand designer, a new colour palette to the owners of Padaria Salgueiro, a six-shop bakery group in Porto, and I will project this page so they can choose between two options. Write the page in European Portuguese. Main palette, six colours: Azul Douro #1F4E79 (signs and aprons), Laranja Brasa #E4572E (offers and buttons), Creme Trigo #F6EBD9 (backgrounds), Verde Alecrim #5B7F5A (organic range), Castanho Forno #4A2F23 (text), Rosa Goiaba #E8A0A0 (seasonal cakes). Calmer alternative: swap Laranja Brasa for Ocre Mel #C98B2B and Rosa Goiaba for Salmão Suave #F0B7A4, and keep the other four. Show every colour as a large block with its name and code, then show both palettes side by side on a sample shop sign, a paper bag and a menu board so the owners can compare them. Under each palette give three pairings that work, for example Castanho Forno text on Creme Trigo. Use the headings Proposta principal, Alternativa mais calma and Decisão, and end with a line for their choice, Paleta A or Paleta B. When the link is shared it should read: Seis cores para as lojas e embalagens da Padaria Salgueiro, com uma alternativa mais calma.

Write the post-mortem for the checkout outage at Northgate Ticketing on 2026-10-09; I'm the engineering director and the readers are our executives, who will go through it on their phones between meetings. Put the short version first: checkout was down for 54 minutes, 18,700 purchases failed, about €212,000 in sales was lost and 1,340 support tickets came in. Cause: a settings change at 14:02 cut the database connection limit on the checkout service from 50 to 5. Then the three fixes, each with its owner and due date: automatic checks on settings changes (Marta Ilves, 2026-10-30), staged rollouts to 5% of traffic first (Rashid Omar, 2026-11-20), and a rollback that needs no manual steps (Priya Naidoo, 2026-10-23). Last, the full timeline, tucked away so that it stays closed until a reader chooses to open it: 14:02 settings change deployed. 14:09 errors rise from 3% to 41% and checkout stops. 14:15 on-call engineer paged. 14:31 first rollback fails. 14:58 manual fix applied. 15:03 checkout recovers. 15:12 all clear confirmed. Keep the tone plain and blameless.

New engineers at Kettle Club, our shared-expenses app, start by reading one small function, split_bill, and I want a page that walks them through it one line at a time; I'm a senior developer there. They will open it on a laptop at their desk on their first day, so each step should show the line, say in plain words what it does, and show the running values for the worked example. The function, by line: 1: def split_bill(total_cents, names): 2:     n = len(names) 3:     if n == 0: 4:         raise ValueError('nobody to split with') 5:     base = total_cents // n 6:     extra = total_cents % n 7:     shares = dict() 8:     for i, name in enumerate(names): 9:         shares[name] = base + (1 if i < extra else 0) 10:     return shares [end of code]. Worked example: 1001 cents shared by Ada, Bo and Cy gives 334, 334 and 333. Add a second example, 90 cents among four people, giving 23, 23, 22 and 22. Finish with the one quirk the team knows about, that the people listed first always get the extra cent. Let the reader try their own total and names to see the split.

Shop owners and printers keep asking how Hazelhoek should look, so I want one brand guideline page for them; I'm the brand manager of Hazelhoek, a Dutch cooperative that sells cycling clothing. They will open it on their phones at the counter or in the print room, from a link in an email. Write the page in Dutch, with the headings Logo, Kleuren, Toon, Doen and Niet doen. The logo is the word Hazelhoek in bold rounded letters in Hazelnoot. Logo rules: never smaller than 24 mm wide in print or 90 pixels on screen; keep clear space around it equal to the height of the letter H; never stretch it, recolour it, or put it on a busy photo. Colours: Hazelnoot #8B5A2B for the logo and headlines, Mosgroen #3F5F3A for buttons, Zandsteen #E9DFCB for backgrounds, Signaalgeel #FFC400 for sale labels only. Tone of voice, three rules: speak plainly, say je and not u, never shout in capitals. Under Doen and Niet doen, show one right and one wrong use of the logo. The sentence that describes the page when its link is shared: Alles wat winkels en drukkers nodig hebben om Hazelhoek goed te laten zien.

Make the third-quarter 2026 report for the board of Ferrow & Dunn Candles; I'm the finance lead, and the board will go through it projected on the wall in the meeting on 2026-11-05, so the main page must stand on its own and the detail must sit in appendices they can skip. Headlines: revenue £5,500k, up 10.7% on £4,970k last year; operating margin 12.4%, up from 11.1%; cash £3,100k. Say in two sentences what drove growth: the West grew fastest, up 24%, and the new wholesale range added £310k. The main page holds the three headline figures, a comparison of revenue by region against last year, and the one decision for the board: whether to open a second warehouse in the West in the first quarter of 2027, costing £460k. Appendix A, revenue by region in £k, this year then last year: North 1,840 and 1,610; South 1,260 and 1,190; East 970 and 1,020; West 1,430 and 1,150. Appendix B, costs in £k: materials 2,050; labour 1,480; freight 520; rent 410; other 358; total 4,818. Mark both appendices as reference only. Keep the tone measured.

Here is an audit of the outside packages used by the dispatch service at Quayside Logistics, which I ran as platform engineer. I will paste the page link into the engineering chat for the six team leads, who will read it on laptops before Monday's planning on 2026-10-26. The list, by line: 1 ledgerkit 4.2.0. 2 tesserae-http 2.3.1. 3 plumbline 0.9.7. 4 owlparse 1.8.2. 5 quillcache 3.1.0. 6 brineq 0.4.4. 7 tallow-ui 5.0.2. 8 gridwright 2.7.9. 9 mothlog 1.2.1. 10 fennel-auth 6.4.0. Findings. Line 2, high: a known flaw, TQ-2026-114, lets an attacker make the service call internal addresses; fixed in 2.3.4. Line 6, high: the licence changed to AGPL, which our policy forbids without legal sign-off. Line 4, medium: no release since 2021-04-09 and no maintainer; five services use it. Line 9, low: two other packages bundle an older copy of mothlog, so two versions ship. The other six lines are clean. Open with a summary: four findings, two high, one medium, one low. Show each finding next to its line with severity, what to do and who owns it: Sana Qureshi for lines 2 and 4, Leo Brandt for lines 6 and 9. High items are due 2026-11-13, the rest 2026-12-04.

Our accessibility committee meets on 2026-10-29 and wants the colour check of the Windrose Transit journey-planner app as a printed page, so it must still read clearly in black and white; I'm the accessibility lead and I measured the colours against our standard: text must reach a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1, and input box borders 3 to 1. Six checks, each with where the colours are used, the colour pair, the measured ratio and my fix: 1. Body text #595959 on white #FFFFFF, 7.0 to 1, passes. 2. Timestamps #949494 on white, 3.0 to 1, fails; change the text to #757575 (4.6 to 1). 3. Delay label, small white text on orange #D9531E, 4.0 to 1, fails; change the orange to #B8400F (5.6 to 1). 4. Links #0B6E99 on white, 5.7 to 1, passes. 5. Confirm button label, white on green #2A6F4F, 6.0 to 1, passes. 6. Input box border #A8A8A8 on white, 2.4 to 1, fails; change it to #8A8A8A (3.4 to 1). Lead with the result, three pass and three fail, then give the table with a small sample of each colour pair. End with the decision I need: approve the three fixes for the release on 2026-11-09.
